title: Press + Analyst Briefing Prep Notes — Production Inference Economics Benchmark (Latency/$)
content:
Purpose
- Prepare Redwood Inference spokespeople for pre-briefs with analysts (and select press) ahead of the public release of our Production Inference Economics Benchmark report.
- Align on: key story, what we can/can’t claim, likely questions, sensitive topics, and approved answers.

Audience
- Industry analysts covering AI infrastructure, LLM platforms, developer platforms, and cloud economics.
- Goal is to help them accurately understand what we measured and why it matters; not to "win" a debate on stage.

Meeting logistics (recommended)
- Format: 30–45 minutes
  - 0–5: context + agenda
  - 5–15: narrative (why inference economics + what we built)
  - 15–30: methodology + top findings (high level)
  - 30–45: Q&A
- Attendees (internal):
  - Primary: Soojin Lee (PMM) + Jonas Weber (Perf/Evals)
  - Optional: Claire Dubois (methodology deep dive), Ethan Wallace (narrative), Michael Grant/Sofia Mendes (only if requested)
- Materials:
  - 1-pager overview (internal)
  - Methodology summary (public-facing)
  - Interactive landing page preview (if stable)
  - PDF preview with placeholders if charts not final

Embargo + sharing rules
- Treat all numbers as embargoed until public launch date/time (TBD by Comms).
- OK to share:
  - Narrative: why "latency/$" and what it indicates
  - Methodology principles and what we will publish (configs, regions, prompt-set mix, caveats)
  - Product framing (Hosted, Dedicated, Private) and how customers use it
- Not OK to share pre-launch:
  - Specific rank-orderings across providers or any unpublished charts/tables
  - Screenshots with numbers unless explicitly approved for that analyst
- If asked for raw data: approved answer is "We will publish a reproducible methodology summary and versioned result artifacts; for raw logs/manifests we can discuss under appropriate access terms." Do not promise.

Key story (message spine)
1) The market has shifted from "Which model?" to "How do you serve it reliably and economically?"
   - In production, outcomes are constrained by latency SLOs, cost ceilings, and variance across regions and workloads.

2) We’re publishing a benchmark focused on production inference economics, not a single vanity metric.
   - Latency/$ is meant to capture an engineering reality: teams optimize for user-perceived speed under a budget.
   - We present supporting metrics (p50/p95 latency, throughput, $/1M tokens) and clear caveats.

3) We’re putting our methodology forward as a first-class artifact.
   - Workloads are defined and repeatable.
   - Stability gates and rerun thresholds reduce noise.
   - We provide configurations and exclusions.

4) Redwood’s differentiation isn’t "a magic model"—it’s predictable serving across environments.
   - Same operational surface across Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployments.
   - Observability + rollouts + reliability/fallbacks are part of serving economics.

What we want analysts to repeat (sound bites)
- “Latency/$ is a practical way to talk about production economics—speed under a cost envelope.”
- “They publish the methodology and caveats, which is unusual for vendor benchmarks.”
- “The emphasis is on repeatability and variance, not best-case hero numbers.”

What we are not trying to do
- Declare a universal winner across all workloads.
- Claim the benchmark reflects every customer’s traffic.
- Over-index on a single model or cherry-picked region.

Definitions (keep consistent)
- Latency/$: a normalized metric that combines end-to-end latency with the effective cost of serving tokens for a defined workload.
- End-to-end latency: includes queueing + runtime + network overhead within the test harness constraints (exact definition in methodology summary).
- Workload: defined mix of prompt sizes (prefill) and generation lengths (decode), with specified concurrency levels.
- Regions: measured in select NA/EU/APAC regions where capacity is available; we disclose which.

Methodology highlights to emphasize (high level)
- Workload realism:
  - Prompt set designed to reflect common production distributions (mixture of prefill-heavy and decode-heavy requests).
  - Multiple context lengths and generation lengths; no single "easy" case.
- Concurrency and backpressure:
  - We test across defined concurrency points; results include p50 and p95, not just average.
- Warmups and caching/batching:
  - We explicitly define caching and batching policy in the report.
  - We avoid unpublished "special" settings; we disclose what is enabled.
- Stability:
  - Repeat runs and reruns when variance exceeds thresholds.
  - Exclusions are documented (e.g., failed runs, regions with insufficient reserved capacity).
- Reproducibility:
  - Versioned artifacts and run manifests; dockerized runner for deterministic reruns.

Sensitive areas + approved guidance
1) Competitor comparisons
- Sensitivity: legal risk + fairness critiques.
- Approved language:
  - “Where we provide context on other providers, we are careful to describe it as directional and workload-dependent, and we document assumptions.”
  - “Our primary goal is to be transparent about Redwood performance and methodology; comparisons are secondary and caveated.”
- Do NOT say:
  - “Fastest,” “best,” “#1,” “industry-leading” unless the specific statement is explicitly approved with substantiation and scope qualifiers.

2) Metric interpretation (latency/$ can be misunderstood)
- Likely critique: “Latency/$ is made up” or “hides tokens/sec.”
- Approved answer:
  - “Tokens/sec is useful, but in production you’re trading off cost, latency SLOs, and tail behavior. Latency/$ is a composite meant to reflect that tradeoff; we still show the underlying components so readers can interpret it.”

3) Cherry-picking / benchmark gaming
- Approved answer:
  - “We publish the workload definition and the exact settings. We also include multiple regions and multiple workload points, and we document exclusions. If someone thinks a different workload is more representative, the methodology makes it clear how to rerun and compare.”

4) Region variability / capacity constraints
- Approved answer:
  - “Yes, regions vary. That’s one of the points: real production users ship to multiple geographies and feel these differences. We address it by reserving capacity, doing repeat runs, and reporting distributional metrics.”

5) Streaming and tool/function calling
- Sensitivity: not all providers implement streaming or tools the same way.
- Approved answer:
  - “The benchmark focuses on core inference performance on standardized request patterns. We call out what is and isn’t included (e.g., structured outputs, tool calls) because implementation differences can dominate.”

6) Data retention / auditability
- Approved answer:
  - “We retain run configs, manifests, and derived datasets used for public claims per internal policy, with access controls. This is so we can substantiate claims and reproduce results.”

7) Security implications of publishing infra details
- Approved answer:
  - “We do not publish sensitive identifiers or operational details that would create security risk. Artifacts are redacted and reviewed.”

8) Incident risk (if asked about launch readiness)
- If asked about page load reliability / spikes:
  - “We’re treating launch as a production event: caching layer, rate-limit guardrails, and dashboards. If we see issues, we’ll prioritize availability and clarity over flashy interactivity.”

Likely analyst questions (Q) + approved answers (A)
Q: Why should anyone trust a vendor benchmark?
A: “Skepticism is healthy. That’s why our focus is on publishing methodology, definitions, and caveats—so the audience can understand what was measured and reproduce it. We also report variance and stability gates rather than best-case runs.”

Q: Does latency/$ reflect my workload?
A: “Not perfectly—no single benchmark will. We include multiple workload points and publish the prompt mix and concurrency. The intent is to provide a credible directional view and a framework; teams should validate on their own traffic, and we can help set that up.”

Q: Are caching and batching enabled?
A: “We explicitly define and disclose our caching/batching policy in the methodology. The goal is to represent realistic production configurations, and to be transparent about what is enabled so readers can interpret results.”

Q: Are you comparing against closed models, open models, or both?
A: “The report focuses on a curated set of LLMs we can evaluate rigorously. When we provide comparative context, we do it carefully and with caveats, since differences in serving stacks and features can affect results.”

Q: Is this just about speed?
A: “No. The benchmark is about economics under latency constraints, and we also discuss reliability and variance. Production inference is an ops problem as much as a raw-performance problem.”

Q: What’s your business angle—are you trying to sell Dedicated/Private?
A: “We’re being upfront that the benchmark is part of our GTM motion, but the methodology is owned by technical teams and intended to be defensible. We expect it to be useful to anyone evaluating production serving—Hosted, Dedicated, or Private.”

Q: How does this relate to GPU types / hardware availability?
A: “Hardware matters. We disclose the region and configuration details that are relevant to interpretation. The goal is not to abstract away reality, but to document it so the conclusions are scoped correctly.”

Q: Are you publishing raw logs and code?
A: “We’re publishing versioned result artifacts and clear run manifests/methodology. Some components may be shareable; some may remain internal for security and supportability reasons. We’ll be explicit about what’s included.”

Q: What if someone finds different numbers?
A: “That can happen due to workload differences, region capacity, or timing. Our approach is to make the methodology explicit, include stability checks, and be clear about the bounds. If there’s a credible discrepancy under the same settings, we’ll investigate and correct.”

Q: Does the benchmark include model quality/accuracy?
A: “This report is focused on serving economics (latency/cost). We intentionally avoid making quality claims in this benchmark. For quality, we recommend task-specific evals.”

Red lines (do not say)
- Absolute superlatives without scope and approval ("fastest", "cheapest", "best").
- Claims implying universal applicability ("for all workloads").
- Claims that imply competitor intent or internal details ("they throttle", "they can’t batch").
- Any disclosure of non-public region capacity constraints or vendor contract details.

Approved positioning vs hyperscalers and other inference providers
- “Different providers optimize for different things. Our platform is optimized for production serving economics with consistent tooling across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.”
- “We emphasize transparency on performance and methodology so engineers can make informed tradeoffs.”

Suggested closing + CTA (analyst-appropriate)
- “We’d value your feedback on whether the methodology is clear and what you’d want to see in future iterations.”
- “If you want to validate the benchmark assumptions against your client use cases, we can provide a walk-through of the workload definitions and how to reproduce on Redwood.”

Follow-ups / action items after each briefing
- Send: final public links once live (landing page + PDF + methodology).
- Capture: analyst questions we couldn’t answer, plus any phrasing they found confusing.
- Log: any requested clarifications (e.g., streaming definition, concurrency choice) and route to Jonas/Claire for potential FAQ updates.

Spokesperson prep checklist (quick)
- Use the same metric names as the report (latency/$, p50, p95, $/1M tokens).
- Repeat the caveat: "workload- and region-dependent".
- If asked for ranking: redirect to methodology and scope; avoid off-the-cuff comparisons.
- If you don’t know: “Let me verify and follow up”—do not improvise numbers.

Notes / open questions (for internal alignment)
- Confirm which charts (if any) are approved for pre-brief sharing under embargo.
- Confirm final list of regions/models that are "supported" vs "experimental" for publication.
- Confirm final legal-approved disclaimer block for slides and any pre-brief PDF.
- Confirm whether we will offer an analyst-only appendix (e.g., extended methodology details) vs keeping a single public artifact.
